headline: Schumer and Van Hollen, rivals for Senate leader, differ on cannabis
dek: With Democrats taking the Senate, Chuck Schumer's legalization bills and Chris Van Hollen's call to deschedule frame what the next leader may bring to a vote.
key_points: Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, who won the majority in this month's midterms; both back cannabis reform.
Schumer has sponsored federal legalization bills since 2018 but never brought a committee-passed banking bill to the floor when he last ran the Senate.
Van Hollen has not cosponsored Schumer's legalization bill but has called for descheduling and voted for the banking bill in committee in 2023.
On hemp they split last year, when Van Hollen voted to keep the THC ban in spending law and Schumer did not; this year both voted to protect a delay of the ban.
body: Senate Democrats won the chamber in this month's midterms, and the fight over who leads them now has a cannabis angle. Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York is being challenged by Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Marijuana Moment laid out both records on 16 November: each supports reform, but they have backed it in different ways and with different intensity.

For the industry, the leader matters more than any single bill. The majority leader decides what reaches the Senate floor, and the cannabis banking bill that cleared committee in 2023 never got a floor vote under Schumer. Whoever wins controls that gate from January.

Schumer has filed comprehensive bills to legalize, tax and regulate cannabis federally several times, most recently the Cannabis Administration and Opportunity Act this year and in 2022 and 2024, after an earlier Marijuana Freedom and Opportunity Act in 2018 and 2019. He has also cosponsored narrower bills to protect state medical cannabis programmes, open banking access and legalize industrial hemp.

His record as majority leader is the sore point. He repeatedly said he supported the banking bill but never brought it to the floor, drawing sharp criticism from industry advocates. He and his allies blame Republican leaders, whose cooperation is usually needed to move bills under Senate rules. Schumer also said in 2021 that he wanted banking reform to move together with broader legalization and expungement, a package that never came together. He did pass one limited reform as leader: the 2022 law easing barriers to cannabis research.
Marijuana Moment notes his focus has faded. Democrats refiled the legalization bill this year without a press event, and Schumer has posted far less about cannabis since 2024.
> The next majority leader will decide whether cannabis banking finally gets a Senate floor vote. That gatekeeping role matters more than either candidate's speeches.
## Van Hollen: descheduling, but not Schumer's bill

Van Hollen has not cosponsored Schumer's legalization bills, but he has called separately for descheduling cannabis, which would remove it from the Controlled Substances Act altogether. He has signed on to bills protecting state medical programmes and encouraging Veterans Affairs research into cannabis for veterans.

In 2023 he voted for the banking bill in the Senate Banking Committee, calling it a step toward ending the cash economy in states like Maryland. He added that if the committee had jurisdiction over criminal justice, he would not back banking reform without addressing those issues too. In the House he consistently voted for amendments protecting state medical cannabis laws, including in 2003 to 2007 and 2012 to 2015, and cosponsored bills to let VA doctors recommend cannabis.

On hemp the two have not always voted together. Last year Van Hollen voted to table an amendment that would have stripped the hemp THC recriminalization language from spending legislation, citing concern about unregulated synthetic hemp products marketed to children, while saying Congress should keep a path for products like CBD. Schumer voted against tabling it, siding with the effort to remove the ban. This year both supported tabling an amendment that would have stripped language delaying the ban from a different bill, which kept the delay in place.

That matters now. The ban's main provisions take effect on 11 December, and as we reported on 14 November, senators remain split on whether to change course. A Democratic leader sympathetic to hemp farmers but wary of intoxicating products could shape what, if anything, rides on the next funding bill.
## Context: what the Senate is already weighing

The leadership race comes as a Senate appropriations panel proposed keeping protections for state medical programmes without the House's anti-rescheduling language, which we covered on 13 November. With the Trump administration's partial rescheduling already in force for state-licensed medical cannabis, the questions for 2027 are banking, hemp and whether Congress acts on broader legalization at all.

The date of the Senate Democratic leadership vote, and any commitments either candidate makes on floor time for cannabis banking. Watch also the hemp language in the next continuing resolution before 11 December, and whether the new majority reintroduces banking legislation early in the 2027 session.
